chapter.name: How the Land Becomes Sacred
chapter.blurb: Sacredness, sacred places of many faiths, pilgrimage, Nature as sacred, sacred geography, rivers and the Kumbh Mela, groves and protecting the sacred.

scope_in.item: Rivers, sangams and the Kumbh Mela

concepts.name: Sacredness and sacred places of different faiths
concepts.description: The meaning of sacredness, and the sacred places of Buddhism, Sikhism, Jainism and religions that came from outside India.
concepts.idea: Every school of thought in India has sacred places, often linked to great figures.
concepts.rule: Sacredness is finding something of deep religious or spiritual significance, worthy of respect and reverence. It can be a place, a journey or even a whole land. Followers of Islam, Christianity, Judaism and Zoroastrianism have shrines such as the Dargah Sharif of Ajmer and the Velankanni Church. Buddhist sites include the Great Stupa at Sanchi and the Mahabodhi Stupa at Bodh Gaya, which gets over four million visitors a year. Sikh takhts include Takht Sri Patna Sahib, the Akal Takht and Takht Sri Keshgarh Sahib. Jain tirthas mark where Tirthankaras attained liberation, such as Mount Abu, Girnar and Shatrunjaya.
concepts.example: Followers of other faiths also visit the Dargah Sharif of Ajmer and the Velankanni Church.

concepts.name: Pilgrimage and tirthayatra
concepts.description: The meaning of tirtha and pilgrimage, the tradition of tirthayatras and examples such as Sabarimala and the Pandharpur wari.
concepts.idea: A pilgrimage is both a physical and an inner journey, practised for thousands of years.
concepts.rule: Many Indians undertake tirthayatras to sacred sites (tirthas). A tirtha literally means a place to cross a river and symbolically a crossing from worldly life to a higher life. The pilgrimage is an inner journey with a code of conduct and has been made for at least 3,000 years without modern transport. Jain tirthas mark places connected with Tirthankaras. Sabarimala in Kerala draws over ten million devotees a year and is reached by a difficult trek symbolising the difficulties of the inner path. The Pandharpur wari in Maharashtra is an 800-year-old annual walk of 21 days to the Vithoba temple.
concepts.example: A group from villages near Lucknow went on a three-month pilgrimage to Rameswaram.

concepts.name: Nature as sacred: Mother Earth and tribal traditions
concepts.description: Hindu, folk and tribal views of Nature as sacred, Bhudevi, and examples from Niyamgiri, Sikkim and the Nilgiris.
concepts.idea: Many traditions treat mountains, rivers and trees as divine, so the whole Earth is sacred.
concepts.rule: In Hindu and many folk and tribal traditions mountains, rivers, trees, plants, animals and stones are sacred, and many rivers are devis. The whole Earth is Mother Earth or Bhudevi. The Niyam Dongar hill in Odisha is sacred to the Dongria Khond tribe as the abode of Niyam Raja and cutting trees there is prohibited. In the early 2000s Sikkim identified sacred mountains, caves, lakes, rocks and hot springs for protection. The Todas of the Nilgiris regard mountain peaks, plants, Shola forests, wetlands and even stones as sacred.
concepts.example: The Toda people regard many mountain peaks as sacred and link them with their gods.

concepts.name: Sacred geography: char dham, jyotirlingas and Shakti pithas
concepts.description: Networks of sacred places across India, the story of the Shakti pithas and how pilgrimage promoted cultural integration.
concepts.idea: Networks of shrines cover all India, so the whole land becomes sacred and people integrate culturally.
concepts.rule: The char dham are four sites in the southern, northern, eastern and western corners of India. The 12 jyotirlingas are shrines to Shiva. The 51 Shakti pithas are places where the body parts of Sati fell after Vishnu cut her body with his chakra; the symbol is that the whole land becomes the divine mother's body. These networks crisscross India, creating a sacred geography. Pilgrims meet diverse languages, foods and customs and notice commonalities. Travellers such as merchants, teachers and debaters met along the routes, exchanging goods and ideas, which helped the cultural integration of the Subcontinent.
concepts.example: The char dham sites are placed at the four corners of India.

concepts.name: Rivers, sangams and the Kumbh Mela
concepts.description: Worship of rivers, the nadistuti sukta, sangams and the Kumbh Mela with its legend and places.
concepts.idea: Rivers are worshipped as lifelines, and the Kumbh Mela at four places draws millions.
concepts.rule: Rivers have been worshipped since Vedic times; the nadistuti sukta of the Rigveda praises 19 major rivers of the northwest. A verse invokes Ganga, Yamuna, Godavari, Sarasvati, Narmada, Sindhu and Kaveri in water. Rivers are addressed with respect, as Ganga ji. Tirthas are often on riverbanks. Prayag is at the confluence of the Ganga, Yamuna and the invisible Sarasvati and hosts the Kumbh Mela every six years. The legend of amrita manthana says drops of nectar fell at Haridwar, Prayagraj, Nashik and Ujjain. About 660 million people took part in the 2025 Kumbh. UNESCO listed it as intangible heritage.
concepts.example: Prayag lies at the sangam of three rivers.

concepts.name: Sacred mountains, trees, groves and protecting the sacred
concepts.description: Mountains and forests as sacred, the peepul, sacred groves, pilgrimage and trade routes, sacred geography elsewhere and conservation.
concepts.idea: Sacred groves and mountains conserve nature, and reverence for the sacred supports sustainability.
concepts.rule: Mountains are symbolic gateways from earth to heaven, so many tirthas lie on hilltops. The peepul (Ficus religiosa) is sacred to Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism and Jainism; the Bodh Gaya tree is cited as a descendant of the Buddha's tree. Sacred groves, such as kavu in Malayalam and sarna in Jharkhand, protect forests from hunting, felling and mining and shelter biodiversity and water bodies, though their numbers are shrinking. Pilgrimage and trade routes often overlap. Elsewhere, the Maori regard Taranaki Maunga as an ancestor and a law gave it rights. Sacred places today are polluted and need protecting.
concepts.example: Grove deities in Thanjavur protect fruit bats, which help pollination and seed dispersal.
